_readme: Vocabulary-only staging file authored by G-A7. No grammar points are authored here; the 154 point ids in DESIGN.md 4.2 belong to G-A1..G-A6 and are only referenced from entry_json.grammar_links. Every entry is entry_json schema_version 2 per DESIGN.md 3.2: >= 3 rotating contexts each with an exact gap_span, register and skill_hook; register and frequency_band at entry level; a confusable where one honestly exists; a chunk block on every chunk and frame; a word_family on words that have one. Deck id prefixes follow the prefixes actually present in data/vocab.jsonl (wrk_, trn_, fud_, crm_) rather than DESIGN.md 4.3's listing, which paraphrases them. Three decks are new beyond the 21 in the pack: academic-core (acw_) for the topic-neutral academic word families the brief asks for, plus frames-written (fw_) and frames-spoken (fs_) as DESIGN.md 3.5 specifies. MERGE NOTE: this file is larger than the 40-entry-per-author allowance in DESIGN.md 4.4 lint 44 because the brief for this block asked for 900+ new entries; the bank-wide floor of 583 in lint 9 is a floor, not a ceiling. COLLISION NOTE for the verify agent: G-A1..G-A6 also author 40 topic-deck entries each using the same <deck-prefix>_<slug> convention, so a duplicate id or lemma between this file and theirs is possible on high-frequency academic words. Every id and lemma here has been checked against data/vocab.jsonl and is unique within this file; cross-author duplicates should be resolved at merge by dropping whichever copy has the weaker contexts.

entry_json.definition: suitable for growing crops, rather than only for grazing animals
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Once the topsoil washes away, arable land takes decades to recover.
example_sentences: Countries with little arable land have to import most of what their people eat.
Building on arable farmland is a decision that cannot be undone.

contexts.text: Once the topsoil washes away, arable land takes decades to recover.
My uncle farms about forty hectares, and only half of it is really arable.
The chart shows a steady fall in the share of arable land between 1990 and 2020.

confusables.difference: Arable says what the land is used for: crops rather than pasture. Fertile says how rich it is. Poor soil can still be arable, and fertile grassland is not.
minimal_pair: The valley floor is arable.
The valley floor is fertile.

entry_json.avoid: Not "arable animals". The word describes land and farming, never livestock.

entry_json.definition: the whole area of land whose rainfall drains into one river or reservoir
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rainfall across the whole catchment feeds a single reservoir north of Verdon.
example_sentences: Tree planting in the upper catchment slows the water down before it reaches the town.
Flood defences work best when the entire catchment is managed as one system.

contexts.text: Rainfall across the whole catchment feeds a single reservoir north of Verdon.
If you pollute anywhere in the catchment, it ends up in the drinking water eventually.
Planning decisions taken upstream affect every household in the catchment below.

entry_json.avoid: In schools and hospitals "catchment area" means the area served, not drainage.

entry_json.definition: the slow process by which land, soil or an ecosystem loses its quality
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Soil degradation is harder to reverse than most people assume.
example_sentences: Decades of overgrazing caused visible degradation along the eastern ridge.
The report links degradation of the coastline to the removal of the dunes.

contexts.text: Soil degradation is harder to reverse than most people assume.
You can see the degradation just by looking at the colour of the fields.
Intensive farming raises yields in the short term and accelerates degradation in the long term.

confusables.difference: Degradation is the standard word for land, soil and ecosystems. Deterioration is the general word for anything getting worse, including health and buildings.
minimal_pair: Land degradation is now measurable.
His health showed a steady deterioration.

entry_json.avoid: Degradation of X, never degradation to X.

entry_json.definition: limited in amount, so it will eventually run out
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fresh water is a finite resource, even in countries that never think about it.
example_sentences: Oil is finite, and every government knows roughly when its own fields will empty.
Treating farmland as finite would change how quickly councils approve new estates.

contexts.text: Fresh water is a finite resource, even in countries that never think about it.
My time is finite, so I have to choose what actually matters.
An economy built on finite reserves has to plan for the year they stop paying.

confusables.difference: Finite means there is an end. Infinite means there is none. Learners often want "unfinite", which does not exist.
minimal_pair: Coal supplies are finite.
The possibilities felt infinite.

entry_json.avoid: Not "finited" or "unfinite". The opposite is infinite.

entry_json.definition: to destroy waste completely by burning it at very high temperature
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Roughly a third of the city's rubbish is incinerated rather than buried.
example_sentences: Incinerating plastic releases substances that filters cannot fully capture.
The plant incinerates waste and sells the heat back to the housing estate beside it.

contexts.text: Roughly a third of the city's rubbish is incinerated rather than buried.
They want to incinerate the waste locally, and nobody living nearby is happy about it.
Waste that cannot be recycled is sorted, dried and then incinerated for heat.

confusables.difference: Incinerate is the technical word for controlled disposal in a furnace. Burn is the everyday word and covers accidental fire too.
minimal_pair: The plant incinerates medical waste.
The barn burned for six hours.

entry_json.avoid: Incinerate takes an object. Rubbish does not "incinerate" by itself.

entry_json.definition: impossible to undo or return to how it was
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Once a species disappears, the loss is irreversible, however much money arrives afterwards.
example_sentences: Clearing ancient woodland does irreversible harm that replanting cannot repair.
Governments hesitate because the decision is expensive and irreversible.

contexts.text: Once a species disappears, the loss is irreversible, however much money arrives afterwards.
The damage to his hearing was irreversible, which is why he wears protection now.
Scientists disagree about the point at which warming becomes irreversible.

entry_json.avoid: Not "unreversible". The prefix is ir- before r.

entry_json.definition: a chemical used to kill insects and other pests that damage crops
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Heavy pesticide use protects the harvest and quietly kills the insects that pollinate it.
example_sentences: Some pesticides stay in the soil long after the crop has been harvested.
Farmers who cut pesticide use often accept a smaller but more reliable yield.

contexts.text: Heavy pesticide use protects the harvest and quietly kills the insects that pollinate it.
I buy organic vegetables when I can afford them, mainly because of the pesticides.
Pesticide sales rose sharply in the first decade and then levelled off.

confusables.difference: A pesticide kills things that eat the crop. A fertiliser feeds the crop. Both are sprayed on fields, which is why learners swap them.
minimal_pair: They sprayed pesticide to stop the beetles.
They spread fertiliser to raise the yield.

entry_json.avoid: Countable: one pesticide, several pesticides.

entry_json.definition: to make damaged or flooded land usable again
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The docks were reclaimed and turned into flats within a decade.
example_sentences: Reclaimed industrial land is cheaper to build on than farmland, and less controversial.
It takes years to reclaim a site where heavy metals have soaked into the soil.

contexts.text: The docks were reclaimed and turned into flats within a decade.
They want to reclaim the old quarry and plant it as woodland.
Land reclaimed from the estuary now carries a third of the city's housing.

confusables.difference: Reclaim means make the land usable, often for something new. Restore means put it back the way it was.
minimal_pair: The quarry was reclaimed as a business park.
The marsh was restored to its original state.

entry_json.avoid: Reclaim also means "get back" — reclaim your luggage. Context decides.

entry_json.definition: the ability of a system, place or person to recover after a shock
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Flood resilience is cheaper to design in than to add afterwards.
example_sentences: Building resilience means accepting that some floods will happen anyway.
Diverse crops give a farm more resilience than a single high-yield variety.

contexts.text: Flood resilience is cheaper to design in than to add afterwards.
What surprised me was the resilience of the people, not the scale of the damage.
A town with one employer has very little economic resilience.

confusables.difference: Resilience is recovering after the shock lands. Resistance is stopping it landing at all. A wall resists water; a town recovers.
minimal_pair: The coast is building resilience.
The coast is building resistance.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not "a resilience" or "resiliences".

entry_json.definition: a situation in which there is not enough of something people need
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Water scarcity already shapes farming decisions across the drier south.
example_sentences: Scarcity of housing pushes rents up faster than any other single factor.
A drought creates scarcity within weeks, and rebuilding supplies takes years.

contexts.text: Water scarcity already shapes farming decisions across the drier south.
We never think about scarcity here, because the shelves are always full.
Price rises are usually the first visible sign of scarcity.

confusables.difference: Scarcity is the abstract condition and suits academic writing. A shortage is a specific gap in a specific place at a specific time.
minimal_pair: Water scarcity is a structural problem.
There was a shortage of bottled water on Tuesday.

entry_json.avoid: Scarcity of X, never scarcity in X.

entry_json.definition: waste water and human waste carried away from homes in pipes
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Untreated sewage entering rivers is a public health problem before it is an environmental one.
example_sentences: Older cities carry sewage and rainwater in the same pipe, which is why storms cause spills.
Investing in sewage treatment is unglamorous and saves more lives than most projects.

contexts.text: Untreated sewage entering rivers is a public health problem before it is an environmental one.
After heavy rain the sewage just overflows straight into the river.
Sewage is screened, settled and treated biologically before the water is released.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not "a sewage" or "sewages".

entry_json.definition: the responsible care of something you look after for others
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Farmers are increasingly paid for stewardship rather than for output alone.
example_sentences: Stewardship schemes reward hedgerows and wetlands instead of extra hectares of wheat.
The idea behind stewardship is simple: you are holding the land for whoever comes next.

contexts.text: Farmers are increasingly paid for stewardship rather than for output alone.
My grandparents talked about stewardship, though they never used that word.
Good stewardship of a coastline means accepting that some of it will be given up.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable, and it takes of: stewardship of the land.

entry_json.definition: poisonous, and harmful to living things even in small amounts
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Toxic waste from the old plating works is still sealed beneath the car park.
example_sentences: Some cleaning products are toxic enough that the label tells you not to mix them.
Social media can turn toxic within hours when a story goes wrong.

contexts.text: Toxic waste from the old plating works is still sealed beneath the car park.
The atmosphere in that office was completely toxic, so I left after a year.
The compound is toxic to fish at concentrations too low to taste.

entry_json.avoid: Toxic to something, never toxic for something.

entry_json.definition: an area of land that is permanently or seasonally covered by shallow water
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Coastal wetlands absorb storm surges that would otherwise reach the houses behind them.
example_sentences: Draining wetlands for farmland removed the flood protection the villages relied on.
A restored wetland stores carbon and cleans water at the same time.

contexts.text: Coastal wetlands absorb storm surges that would otherwise reach the houses behind them.
We spent a morning walking round a wetland reserve, and I saw birds I'd never seen before.
The area of protected wetland doubled over the twenty-year period.

entry_json.avoid: Usually plural when general: wetlands are, not wetland is.

entry_json.definition: plant or animal material burned or processed as a source of energy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Biomass accounted for a small but rising share of the country's heat supply.
example_sentences: Burning biomass releases carbon that the next crop is supposed to absorb again.
Biomass suits rural heating far better than it suits city electricity.

contexts.text: Biomass accounted for a small but rising share of the country's heat supply.
The whole village is heated by a biomass boiler, which sounds odd until you see it.
Whether biomass counts as clean energy depends entirely on where the wood came from.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not "biomasses".

entry_json.definition: a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere and warms the planet
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Transport is now the largest single source of greenhouse gas emissions in many countries.
example_sentences: Methane is a greenhouse gas that traps far more heat than carbon dioxide does.
Cutting greenhouse gases means changing how we heat buildings, not just how we drive.

contexts.text: Transport is now the largest single source of greenhouse gas emissions in many countries.
Flying is the one thing I do that really adds to greenhouse gas emissions.
Greenhouse gas concentrations rose steadily throughout the period shown.

entry_json.avoid: Before a noun it stays singular: greenhouse gas emissions, not greenhouse gases emissions.

entry_json.definition: releasing no more carbon than is removed again, so the net effect is zero
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council has promised to be carbon neutral within fifteen years.
example_sentences: A carbon neutral building still uses energy; it just balances what it uses.
Claiming to be carbon neutral is easy, and proving it is not.

contexts.text: The council has promised to be carbon neutral within fifteen years.
My company says it's carbon neutral, but most of that is offsetting.
Becoming carbon neutral is far cheaper for a service business than for a steelworks.

confusables.difference: Carbon neutral balances to zero. Carbon negative removes more than it releases, so the balance goes below zero.
minimal_pair: The plant is carbon neutral.
The forest scheme is carbon negative.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenate only before a noun: a carbon-neutral campus, but the campus is carbon neutral.

entry_json.definition: an economic model in which products are reused and recycled instead of thrown away
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A circular economy treats waste as a design fault rather than an inevitable by-product.
example_sentences: In a circular economy, the company that sells you a washing machine also takes it back.
Recycling alone is not a circular economy; it is the last step of a linear one.

contexts.text: A circular economy treats waste as a design fault rather than an inevitable by-product.
The circular economy idea makes sense to me, but repairs still cost more than replacing.
Moving towards a circular economy requires manufacturers to design for repair from the start.

entry_json.avoid: Takes an article: a circular economy, the circular economy.

entry_json.definition: coal, oil or gas, formed underground over millions of years and burned for energy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Countries that export fossil fuels have the least incentive to stop selling them.
example_sentences: Burning fossil fuels is the single largest reason the atmosphere is warming.
Subsidies keep fossil fuels artificially cheap and slow every alternative down.

contexts.text: Countries that export fossil fuels have the least incentive to stop selling them.
We're still paying for fossil fuels every time we fill the car up.
Fossil fuel imports fell by roughly a quarter after the new plants opened.

entry_json.avoid: Plural for the group: fossil fuels are cheap. Singular before a noun: fossil fuel subsidies.

entry_json.definition: plastic designed to be used once and then thrown away
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Several countries have banned single-use plastic cutlery outright.
example_sentences: A charge of a few pence cut single-use plastic bags dramatically within months.
Single-use plastic is convenient, cheap, and almost impossible to recycle profitably.

contexts.text: Several countries have banned single-use plastic cutlery outright.
I try to avoid single-use plastic, though it's hard with fresh food.
Consumption of single-use plastic fell in the two years after the charge was introduced.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenated before the noun. The plastic is single use, but a single-use bag.

entry_json.definition: how clean or polluted the air in a place is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Poor air quality costs cities more in hospital admissions than in lost working days.
example_sentences: Schools near busy roads record the worst air quality in the whole borough.
Air quality is one of the few environmental problems residents can smell.

chunk.shape: air quality + NOUN / ADJ + air quality

contexts.text: Poor air quality costs cities more in hospital admissions than in lost working days.
The air quality near the ring road is noticeably worse in summer.
Air quality improved most sharply in the year the low-emission zone opened.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not "air qualities".

entry_json.definition: the gradual increase in the height of the sea caused by a warming climate
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rising sea levels will reach the low-lying farmland long before they reach the town.
example_sentences: Rising sea levels do not arrive as a flood; they arrive as a slightly worse storm each decade.
Adapting to rising sea levels may mean abandoning some places entirely.

contexts.text: Rising sea levels will reach the low-lying farmland long before they reach the town.
Whole islands are being written off because of rising sea levels, which frightens me.
Coastal defences at Sandmouth were rebuilt in response to rising sea levels.

entry_json.avoid: Normally plural: rising sea levels are, not rising sea level is.

entry_json.definition: a storm, flood, heatwave or drought that is far outside the normal range
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Insurers were the first to notice that extreme weather events had stopped being rare.
example_sentences: One extreme weather event is chance; a pattern of them is something else.
Rural areas recover from extreme weather more slowly because repairs arrive last.

contexts.text: Insurers were the first to notice that extreme weather events had stopped being rare.
We changed our holiday plans twice last year because of extreme weather.
The graph records eleven extreme weather events in the final decade alone.

entry_json.avoid: "Weather" is uncountable, so count the events: three extreme weather events, not three extreme weathers.

entry_json.definition: to stop using or providing something gradually, over a planned period
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The plan is to phase out coal power over eight years rather than close the plants at once.
example_sentences: Governments phase things out when banning them overnight would cost too many jobs.
Phasing out a subsidy is politically harder than never introducing it.

chunk.shape: phase + OBJECT + out / phase out + OBJECT

contexts.text: The plan is to phase out coal power over eight years rather than close the plants at once.
They're going to phase out the old buses, so the fumes should get better.
Diesel vehicles were phased out between 2028 and 2034.

confusables.difference: Phase out is gradual and planned, with a date at the end. Ban is immediate and total. Choose phase out when the sentence mentions a timescale.
minimal_pair: Coal will be phased out by 2035.
Coal was banned last April.

entry_json.avoid: Separable: phase it out, never "phase out it".

entry_json.definition: to use or consume less of something, without stopping completely
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I've been trying to cut down on meat, mostly for health reasons.
example_sentences: Cutting down on short car journeys is the easiest change most families can make.
She cut down on flying without ever deciding to stop completely.

contexts.text: I've been trying to cut down on meat, mostly for health reasons.
Households that cut down on food waste save money before they save anything else.
Advice to cut down on sugar works better than advice to give it up.

confusables.difference: Cut down on means less. Cut out means none at all. The difference matters when a sentence promises a result.
minimal_pair: I've cut down on sugar.
I've cut out sugar entirely.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition on is not optional: cut down on plastic, not cut down plastic.

entry_json.definition: rainwater that flows over the ground into rivers, often carrying pollution with it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Agricultural run-off is the main reason nitrate levels rise after heavy rain.
example_sentences: Green roofs slow run-off down enough to stop the drains overflowing.
Run-off from a single storm can undo a year of river cleaning.

contexts.text: Agricultural run-off is the main reason nitrate levels rise after heavy rain.
All the run-off from the fields ends up in the same stream we swim in.
Paving front gardens increases run-off and pushes water into the drains all at once.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable in this sense. Hyphenated as a noun; the verb is two words, run off.

entry_json.definition: used to say that one thing was gained by damaging or losing another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Industrial growth arrived quickly, at the expense of the rivers that ran through it.
example_sentences: Protecting one industry at the expense of another is a choice, not an accident.
Speed came at the expense of accuracy, and the errors took months to find.
collocations: growth at the expense of the environment
at the expense of the poorest

chunk.shape: X happens at the expense of Y

contexts.text: Industrial growth arrived quickly, at the expense of the rivers that ran through it.
I got promoted, but honestly it was at the expense of seeing my family.
Cheap food is produced at the expense of the soil it is grown in.

confusables.difference: At the expense of says one thing was damaged so the other could happen. Instead of just says one replaced the other, with no harm implied.
minimal_pair: Growth came at the expense of clean air.
They planted trees instead of grass.

entry_json.avoid: Always the expense, never "at expense of".

entry_json.definition: the effect an activity has on the natural world, good or bad
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Every large project must now assess its environmental impact before planning permission is granted.
example_sentences: Reducing environmental impact usually means designing differently, not working harder.
An environmental impact assessment can delay a project by two years.

chunk.shape: VERB + the environmental impact of + NOUN

contexts.text: Every large project must now assess its environmental impact before planning permission is granted.
Nobody talks about the environmental impact of all the data centres.
The environmental impact of a new runway is easier to measure than its economic benefit.

entry_json.avoid: The impact of X on Y. Impact on, never impact to.

entry_json.definition: a strip of natural land that lets animals move safely between two habitats
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A wildlife corridor across the motorway costs less than the reserve it connects.
example_sentences: Without wildlife corridors, a protected wood becomes an island that slowly empties.
Hedgerows worked as wildlife corridors for centuries before anyone named them.

contexts.text: A wildlife corridor across the motorway costs less than the reserve it connects.
They've planted a wildlife corridor along the old railway line, which I think is clever.
Populations in isolated woods declined until a wildlife corridor linked them.

entry_json.avoid: Countable: a wildlife corridor, several wildlife corridors.

entry_json.definition: to cause more damage than benefit, despite good intentions
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Releasing captive-bred birds without restoring the habitat can do more harm than good.
example_sentences: Planting the wrong trees in a wetland does more harm than good.
She worried that speaking up would do more harm than good, so she said nothing.
collocations: may do more harm than good
end up doing more harm than good

chunk.shape: X does more harm than good

contexts.text: Releasing captive-bred birds without restoring the habitat can do more harm than good.
Taking supplements you don't need probably does more harm than good.
A subsidy that keeps failing farms open may do more harm than good in the long run.

entry_json.avoid: Fixed comparative: more harm than good, never "more harm than better".

entry_json.definition: an amount so small that it makes almost no difference to the problem
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Recycling at home feels like a drop in the ocean compared with what industry produces.
example_sentences: The donation was welcome, but everyone knew it was a drop in the ocean.
Twenty new buses is a drop in the ocean in a city of two million.
collocations: be a drop in the ocean
little more than a drop in the ocean

chunk.shape: X is a drop in the ocean

contexts.text: Recycling at home feels like a drop in the ocean compared with what industry produces.
The fund is generous in isolation and a drop in the ocean beside the damage.
One country's emissions cuts are a drop in the ocean unless its neighbours act too.

entry_json.avoid: Fixed: in the ocean, not "in an ocean" or "of the ocean".

entry_json.definition: to cause gradual damage to something over a period of time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Decades of heavy lorries have taken their toll on the coastal road.
example_sentences: The drought took its toll on farms that had survived every previous dry summer.
Years of underfunding have taken their toll on the rail network.
collocations: take its toll on the environment

chunk.shape: X takes its toll on Y

contexts.text: Decades of heavy lorries have taken their toll on the coastal road.
The night shifts really took their toll on my sleep.
Mass tourism takes its toll on exactly the places people travel to see.

entry_json.avoid: The possessive agrees with the subject: they took their toll, it took its toll.

entry_json.definition: to suffer the worst part of something unpleasant
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Low-lying districts bear the brunt of the flooding while the decisions are taken uphill.
example_sentences: Coastal villages bore the brunt of the storm and waited two years for repairs.
Junior staff bore the brunt of the reorganisation.
collocations: bear the brunt of the damage
bear the brunt of the cuts

chunk.shape: X bears the brunt of Y

contexts.text: Low-lying districts bear the brunt of the flooding while the decisions are taken uphill.
Families on the lowest incomes bear the brunt of every price rise.
Countries that emit least often bear the brunt of the consequences.

entry_json.avoid: Bear, bore, borne. Not "bare the brunt".

entry_json.definition: protected open land around a city where building is restricted
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Releasing green belt land solves the housing shortage and creates a different problem.
example_sentences: Green belt policy pushed development outwards rather than stopping it.
Every city with a green belt eventually argues about the edge of it.

contexts.text: Releasing green belt land solves the housing shortage and creates a different problem.
They want to build on the green belt, and half the village is against it.
The green belt around Norland has not been redrawn since it was designated.

confusables.difference: A green belt is a planning designation around a city. Green space is any park or open ground, including inside the city.
minimal_pair: They built on the green belt.
The estate has almost no green space.

entry_json.avoid: Usually with the: the green belt. Hyphenate before a noun: green-belt land.

entry_json.definition: the largest number of people or animals an area can support without damage
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Visitor numbers now exceed the carrying capacity of the footpaths themselves.
example_sentences: Nobody agrees on a figure for carrying capacity until the damage is already visible.
Limiting permits is a blunt way of respecting a site's carrying capacity.
collocations: the carrying capacity of a site

contexts.text: Visitor numbers now exceed the carrying capacity of the footpaths themselves.
The island has a carrying capacity, and in August we're clearly past it.
Once a habitat passes its carrying capacity, the population falls whatever anyone does.

entry_json.avoid: Takes of: the carrying capacity of the reserve.

entry_json.definition: official approval saying that a course or institution meets a required standard
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Without accreditation, a qualification is only as good as the employer's opinion of it.
example_sentences: The college lost its accreditation and its students had to transfer mid-year.
Accreditation matters most in fields where a mistake is dangerous.

contexts.text: Without accreditation, a qualification is only as good as the employer's opinion of it.
I checked the accreditation before I paid for the course, which turned out to be sensible.
Online providers are growing faster than the bodies that grant accreditation.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable in most uses. Not "accreditations" for a single approval.

entry_json.definition: a natural ability that makes someone learn a particular thing quickly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Selecting children at eleven assumes an aptitude that has not finished forming.
example_sentences: She showed an aptitude for numbers long before anyone taught her algebra.
An aptitude test measures what you can pick up, not what you already know.

contexts.text: Selecting children at eleven assumes an aptitude that has not finished forming.
I had no aptitude for languages at school, and I've had to work at it since.
Aptitude tests predict early performance better than they predict a career.

confusables.difference: Aptitude is potential, before training. Ability is what you can do now. A child has an aptitude for music; a pianist has ability.
minimal_pair: He has an aptitude for coding.
He has the ability to code.

entry_json.avoid: Aptitude for something, never aptitude to something.

entry_json.definition: connected with thinking, understanding and remembering
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Reading aloud supports cognitive development in ways screen time does not.
example_sentences: Cognitive skills develop unevenly, which is why age is a poor guide to readiness.
A noisy classroom imposes a cognitive cost that nobody sees on the timetable.

contexts.text: Reading aloud supports cognitive development in ways screen time does not.
Learning an instrument late in life is supposed to slow cognitive decline.
The study measured cognitive performance before and after eight weeks of training.

entry_json.avoid: An adjective only. The noun is cognition, not "cognitive".

entry_json.definition: the ability to understand what you read or hear
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Reading comprehension scores improved faster than spelling scores across the same period.
example_sentences: Comprehension collapses when a text has more than a few unknown words per line.
Listening comprehension improves fastest when the material is slightly too hard.

contexts.text: Reading comprehension scores improved faster than spelling scores across the same period.
My comprehension is much better than my speaking, which is frustrating.
Testing comprehension with multiple choice measures guessing as well as understanding.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable here. Not "a comprehension" or "comprehensions".

entry_json.definition: the list of topics a particular course will cover, and in what order
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Every new priority is added to the syllabus and nothing is ever removed.
example_sentences: The plural is syllabuses, though syllabi is still seen in older writing.
A syllabus written for exams tends to squeeze out everything not examined.

contexts.text: Every new priority is added to the syllabus and nothing is ever removed.
We finished the syllabus two weeks before the exam, which felt like a miracle.
A narrow syllabus raises test scores and lowers the range of what pupils can do.

contexts.text: Teenagers build a digital footprint years before they understand what it is.
Employers check a candidate's digital footprint long before the interview.

entry_json.avoid: Countable and singular per person: your digital footprint.

entry_json.definition: to change or develop as fast as something else is changing

example_sentences: Training budgets rarely keep pace with the systems they are meant to support.
The road network could not keep pace with the number of new houses.
collocations: struggle to keep pace with demand

contexts.text: Regulation has never kept pace with the technology it is supposed to govern.
I find it hard to keep pace with how quickly the tools change.
Wages failed to keep pace with housing costs throughout the period.

I can't keep up with the news.

contexts.gap_span: at the touch of a button

contexts.gap_span: at the touch of a button

entry_json.definition: something that has an important advantage and an equally important disadvantage

entry_json.definition: over a long period of time, when the final result becomes clear

collocations: in the long run it pays off

chunk.shape: X will happen in the long run

entry_json.definition: to have a serious disadvantage that you have to accept

contexts.text: All that convenience comes at a price, and the price is our data.

entry_json.avoid: At a price, not "with a price" or "at the price".

entry_json.definition: to be able to use or reach something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Not everyone in my class had access to a computer at home.
example_sentences: Gaining access to the data took eighteen months of requests.
Access to a library changes a child's chances more than any single lesson.

contexts.text: Not everyone in my class had access to a computer at home.
Roughly a third of rural households still do not have access to a reliable connection.
Patients who have access to their own records ask better questions.

entry_json.avoid: Access to something, never "access of" or "access at".

entry_json.definition: to use all of something so that none is left

example_sentences: The laptop ran out of storage halfway through the project.
We ran out of options and chose the least bad one.

contexts.text: I always run out of time in exams, which is why I practise with a clock.
Countries do not run out of water suddenly; they run short of it every summer.
Households that run out of savings turn to credit, and the cost compounds.

entry_json.avoid: Of is required before the noun: run out of time, not "run out time".

entry_json.definition: using the most advanced technology currently available
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A state-of-the-art scanner is useless in a hospital with nobody trained to read it.
example_sentences: The laboratory was state of the art in 2010 and is unremarkable now.
Buying state-of-the-art equipment is the easy half of modernising anything.

contexts.text: A state-of-the-art scanner is useless in a hospital with nobody trained to read it.
The new centre has state-of-the-art equipment, and it's usually empty.
State-of-the-art facilities attract researchers, and researchers attract funding.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenated before a noun; unhyphenated after be: it is state of the art.

entry_json.definition: made or arranged exactly to suit a particular person or purpose
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The training was tailor-made for our team, so nothing felt wasted.
example_sentences: The job seemed tailor-made for her, and she still turned it down.
Tailor-made solutions are unaffordable at scale, which is why standards exist.

contexts.text: The training was tailor-made for our team, so nothing felt wasted.
A tailor-made programme costs more and finishes far sooner.
Treatment that is tailor-made to the individual is the direction most medicine is taking.

entry_json.avoid: Tailor-made for someone or something, never "tailor-made to someone".

entry_json.definition: containing or using the newest information or version

contexts.text: I try to stay up to date with the news without reading it all day.
Systems that are not kept up to date are the ones attackers find first.
Keeping patient records up to date matters more than the format they are stored in.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenate before a noun: an up-to-date record. No hyphens after be: it is up to date.

entry_json.definition: material posted online by ordinary users rather than by a company
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Platforms built on user-generated content avoid the cost of making anything.
example_sentences: User-generated reviews shape more purchases than advertising does.
The value of user-generated content is that it is free, and so is its main problem.

contexts.text: Platforms built on user-generated content avoid the cost of making anything.

Moderating user-generated content at scale is a problem nobody has solved cheaply.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Hyphenate the compound adjective before the noun.

entry_json.definition: the present period, in which most information is stored and shared electronically
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Privacy in the digital age means something different from privacy behind a front door.
example_sentences: In the digital age, forgetting has become harder than remembering.
The digital age arrived unevenly, and some places are still waiting.

contexts.text: Privacy in the digital age means something different from privacy behind a front door.
Handwriting still matters to me, even in the digital age.
Attention has become the scarce resource of the digital age.

entry_json.avoid: Always with the: in the digital age.

entry_json.definition: to create the conditions that make something else possible later
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap sensors paved the way for a generation of devices nobody had imagined.
example_sentences: The rail link paved the way for four new towns along the valley.

collocations: pave the way for a breakthrough

chunk.shape: X paves the way for Y

contexts.text: Cheap sensors paved the way for a generation of devices nobody had imagined.
That one discovery paved the way for everything that came after it.
Early trials paved the way for a treatment that reached patients a decade later.

entry_json.avoid: For, not "to": pave the way for something.

entry_json.definition: to develop or progress more slowly than others
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Regions that lag behind in transport tend to fall short in wages a decade later.
example_sentences: Skills training lags behind the industries it is supposed to serve.

contexts.text: Regions that lag behind in transport tend to fall short in wages a decade later.

Broadband speeds lagged behind the European average until 2019.

confusables.difference: Fall behind describes becoming late or slipping from a position you held. Lag behind describes being persistently slower than others, often for years.
minimal_pair: Wages lagged behind prices.
He fell behind with the rent.

entry_json.avoid: Behind is not optional: lag behind, not "lag the others".

entry_json.definition: to learn how to do something after a bit of practice
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me about a week to get the hang of the new system.
example_sentences: Once you get the hang of the layout, the rest is straightforward.
She got the hang of cycling in an afternoon and has never stopped.

contexts.text: It took me about a week to get the hang of the new system.
Most staff get the hang of a new tool quickly and never use half of it.
Learners who get the hang of one method transfer it to the next more easily.

entry_json.avoid: Fixed: the hang of, never "a hang of".

entry_json.definition: to remove small problems or differences from something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We spent two months ironing out problems that should have been caught earlier.
example_sentences: They ironed out the timetable clashes before the term started.
Ironing out the last five per cent of the faults takes half the budget.

contexts.text: We spent two months ironing out problems that should have been caught earlier.
Every system needs a year of use before the last faults are ironed out.
Negotiators ironed out the differences that had blocked the agreement for years.

entry_json.avoid: Separable: iron them out, or iron out the problems.

entry_json.definition: to do something quickly and cheaply by leaving out important steps

example_sentences: Cutting corners on the foundations is the one mistake you cannot fix later.

Firms that cut corners on safety usually save less than a single accident costs.

entry_json.avoid: No article: cut corners, never "cut the corners" in this sense.

entry_json.definition: sometimes good and sometimes bad, with no reliable pattern
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The signal out there is hit and miss, so I never rely on it.

collocations: the quality is hit and miss

contexts.text: The signal out there is hit and miss, so I never rely on it.
Automatic subtitles remain hit and miss with any accent the system rarely hears.
A test that is hit and miss may be worse than no test at all.

entry_json.avoid: Also written hit-or-miss. No article: it is hit and miss.

entry_json.definition: an illness that is not serious, especially a long-standing one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Pharmacies could treat most minor ailments and free up appointments for everything else.
example_sentences: A cough that lasts three days is an ailment; a cough that lasts three months is not.

contexts.text: Pharmacies could treat most minor ailments and free up appointments for everything else.

confusables.difference: An ailment is minor and often vague. A disease is a named condition with a known cause or course. Nobody calls cancer an ailment.

entry_json.avoid: Countable, and usually plural: minor ailments.

entry_json.definition: to make pain, suffering or a problem less severe

A second bridge would alleviate the congestion rather than remove it.

confusables.difference: Alleviate reduces something. Cure ends it completely. Choose alleviate when the problem remains and only its severity changes.
minimal_pair: The drug alleviates the pain.
The drug cures the infection.

entry_json.avoid: Alleviate takes an object: alleviate pain. Not "the pain alleviated".

entry_json.definition: able to be passed from one person to another

entry_json.definition: making someone very weak and unable to do normal things

entry_json.definition: passed from parents to children through their genes

entry_json.definition: how often a disease or event occurs in a population

entry_json.definition: relieving symptoms without curing the illness itself

entry_json.definition: likely to be affected or harmed by something

entry_json.definition: helping to treat an illness, or simply making you feel better

entry_json.definition: to be likely to suffer from something or do something, repeatedly

entry_json.definition: slightly unwell, without anything serious being wrong
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I've been a bit under the weather all week, nothing serious.
example_sentences: She was under the weather for a fortnight and blamed the change of season.
He seemed under the weather, so we finished the meeting early.

contexts.text: I've been a bit under the weather all week, nothing serious.
Staff who feel under the weather and come in anyway spread more than they contribute.
Reporting oneself as under the weather is not the same as being ill enough to record.

entry_json.avoid: Fixed: under the weather, never "under weather".

entry_json.definition: a medical examination to make sure you are healthy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I go for a check-up once a year, and I've never enjoyed a single one.
example_sentences: A five-minute check-up caught something that had shown no symptoms at all.
Booking a check-up is easy; going to it is apparently much harder.

contexts.text: I go for a check-up once a year, and I've never enjoyed a single one.
Free annual check-ups find some problems early and worry a great many healthy people.
Attendance at routine check-ups falls sharply as travel time rises.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenated as a noun: a check-up. Two words as a verb: check up on someone.

entry_json.definition: to be taken into hospital as a patient
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Patients admitted to hospital at weekends waited longer for a specialist.
example_sentences: She was admitted on the Friday and discharged the following Tuesday.
Emergency admissions rise every year in the same fortnight of January.

contexts.text: Patients admitted to hospital at weekends waited longer for a specialist.
My grandfather was admitted to hospital twice that winter.
Reducing the number of people admitted to hospital is cheaper than adding beds.

entry_json.avoid: British English drops the article: admitted to hospital, not "to the hospital".

entry_json.definition: a way of dealing with something that gives fair weight to each side
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I take a balanced approach to food, which mostly means I don't ban anything.
example_sentences: A balanced approach sounds weak and is usually the only thing that lasts.
The committee took a balanced approach and satisfied nobody entirely.

contexts.text: I take a balanced approach to food, which mostly means I don't ban anything.
A balanced approach to exercise beats an intense one that lasts three weeks.
A balanced approach to regulation protects consumers without closing small firms.

entry_json.avoid: A balanced approach to something, never "a balanced approach for".

entry_json.definition: the damage that happens to something, or someone, through ordinary long use
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Years of running caused a lot of wear and tear on my knees.
example_sentences: The tenancy agreement allows for normal wear and tear but not for holes in the walls.
Wear and tear on the equipment was the largest hidden cost of the whole scheme.

contexts.text: Years of running caused a lot of wear and tear on my knees.
Much of what we call ageing is ordinary wear and tear on joints that were never rested.
Heavy vehicles cause wear and tear on road surfaces out of all proportion to their number.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable and fixed in order: wear and tear, never "tear and wear".

entry_json.definition: a situation where each problem makes the next one worse, and it returns to the start
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Bad sleep makes me anxious and the anxiety ruins my sleep, so it's a vicious circle.
example_sentences: Breaking a vicious circle usually means changing one thing hard rather than everything gently.
Inactivity and low mood form a vicious circle that a short daily walk can interrupt.

contexts.text: Bad sleep makes me anxious and the anxiety ruins my sleep, so it's a vicious circle.
Borrowing to pay interest creates a vicious circle that income alone rarely breaks.
Fewer passengers means fewer buses, which is a vicious circle every rural route knows.

confusables.difference: The same meaning. Circle is the older British form; cycle is more common now and equally acceptable. Do not mix them in one text.
minimal_pair: It became a vicious circle.
It became a vicious cycle.

entry_json.avoid: Vicious, not "vicous". The opposite is a virtuous circle.

entry_json.definition: the process by which separate things gradually become similar or move towards each other
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The convergence of living standards across the region has been slower than governments predicted.
example_sentences: You can see the convergence in how people my age dress, wherever you go.
The chart shows a clear convergence in average income between the two groups after 2005.

word_family.note: the verb, normally followed by on or towards
describes trends that are coming together

contexts.text: The convergence of living standards across the region has been slower than governments predicted.
You can see the convergence in how people my age dress, wherever you go.
The chart shows a clear convergence in average income between the two groups after 2005.

confusables.difference: Convergence is separate things drifting towards each other on their own. Integration is them being joined into one system by a deliberate decision.
minimal_pair: Wages showed a slow convergence over the decade.
The two markets completed their integration in 2010.

entry_json.avoid: Say convergence of X or convergence between X and Y, never convergence to X.

entry_json.definition: to make things become the same as each other, so that local differences disappear
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Global retail chains homogenise high streets until one city centre is hard to tell from another.
example_sentences: I do think travel homogenises places a bit, because everywhere starts serving the same breakfast.
Critics argue that streaming platforms homogenise taste rather than widen it.

word_family.note: describes a group whose members are all alike

contexts.text: Global retail chains homogenise high streets until one city centre is hard to tell from another.
I do think travel homogenises places a bit, because everywhere starts serving the same breakfast.
Critics argue that streaming platforms homogenise taste rather than widen it.

confusables.difference: Homogenise is usually a criticism and means variety was lost. Standardise is usually neutral or positive and means one agreed version was adopted.
minimal_pair: Tourism has homogenised the old quarter.
The board standardised the safety checks across all sites.

entry_json.avoid: Not a synonym for unify. Homogenise removes difference rather than creating agreement.

entry_json.definition: a rapid increase in the number of something, usually more than is wanted
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The proliferation of low-cost carriers has put small regional airports under real strain.
example_sentences: There has been such a proliferation of delivery apps that I have stopped counting them.
The proliferation of unregulated lenders followed the loosening of the rules in 2011.

word_family.note: the verb, used without an object

contexts.text: The proliferation of low-cost carriers has put small regional airports under real strain.
There has been such a proliferation of delivery apps that I have stopped counting them.
The proliferation of unregulated lenders followed the loosening of the rules in 2011.

confusables.difference: Proliferation is about the number of separate things multiplying, and it hints that this is a problem. Growth is about one thing getting bigger, and it is neutral.
minimal_pair: The proliferation of small operators confused travellers.
The growth of the airline surprised its rivals.

entry_json.avoid: Use with a countable plural. Not the proliferation of pollution.

entry_json.definition: the freedom of a country, region or organisation to govern or run itself
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Member states surrender a degree of autonomy in return for access to a single market.
example_sentences: What I liked about that job was the autonomy more than the money.
Regional autonomy over spending was extended in the reforms of the last decade.

contexts.text: Member states surrender a degree of autonomy in return for access to a single market.
What I liked about that job was the autonomy more than the money.
Regional autonomy over spending was extended in the reforms of the last decade.

confusables.difference: Autonomy is self-government inside a larger structure you still belong to. Independence is being outside that structure altogether.
minimal_pair: The province was granted autonomy over education.
The colony declared independence in 1946.

entry_json.avoid: Usually uncountable. Not autonomies unless you mean several separate self-governing regions.

entry_json.definition: the removal of government rules that had controlled how an industry operates
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Deregulation of the energy market was defended as a way of driving prices down.
example_sentences: My dad says the buses got worse straight after deregulation.
Deregulation in the 1980s is widely treated as the starting point of the current system.

word_family.note: the verb, usually passive in this sense
describes a market with the rules removed

contexts.text: Deregulation of the energy market was defended as a way of driving prices down.
My dad says the buses got worse straight after deregulation.
Deregulation in the 1980s is widely treated as the starting point of the current system.

confusables.difference: Deregulation removes the rules while the owner may stay the same. Privatisation changes who owns the thing, and the rules may stay.
minimal_pair: Deregulation let new firms enter the market.
Privatisation transferred the network to shareholders.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not a deregulation.

entry_json.definition: a large group of people who have spread out from their original homeland and settled elsewhere
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The diaspora sends home more money each year than the country earns from exports.
example_sentences: Half my family are part of that diaspora, so we grew up between two places.
Members of the diaspora have kept the language alive far longer than anyone expected.

contexts.text: The diaspora sends home more money each year than the country earns from exports.
Half my family are part of that diaspora, so we grew up between two places.
Members of the diaspora have kept the language alive far longer than anyone expected.

confusables.difference: Diaspora names the settled community abroad. Emigration names the act of leaving.
minimal_pair: The diaspora funds two schools at home.
Emigration rose sharply after the drought.

entry_json.avoid: A diaspora is people, not a place. Not "moved to the diaspora".

entry_json.definition: to make laws or trade rules less strict, so that markets or people can operate more freely
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Countries that liberalise trade quickly often find their weakest industries collapse first.
example_sentences: They liberalised the visa rules last year and my cousin came over almost immediately.
Import rules were liberalised in stages between 1998 and 2004.

word_family.note: in this sense meaning open rather than political

contexts.text: Countries that liberalise trade quickly often find their weakest industries collapse first.
They liberalised the visa rules last year and my cousin came over almost immediately.
Import rules were liberalised in stages between 1998 and 2004.

confusables.difference: Liberalise is what governments do to whole systems of rules. Relax is what anyone does to a single rule and is far less formal.
minimal_pair: The government liberalised the banking sector.
The school relaxed its uniform policy.

entry_json.avoid: Takes an object. Not "the market liberalised" unless you mean it opened by itself.

entry_json.definition: operating across several countries rather than belonging to one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Transnational firms can move profits to wherever the tax is lowest.
example_sentences: It is a transnational problem, so no single government can fix it on its own.
Transnational networks of researchers now produce most of the work in this field.

contexts.text: Transnational firms can move profits to wherever the tax is lowest.
It is a transnational problem, so no single government can fix it on its own.
Transnational networks of researchers now produce most of the work in this field.

confusables.difference: International describes relations between countries that stay separate. Transnational describes something that ignores the borders altogether.
minimal_pair: International talks resumed in March.
Transnational gangs move goods through four countries.

entry_json.avoid: An adjective only. There is no noun a transnational in careful writing.

entry_json.definition: the slow wearing away of something, used of soil and equally of rights, values or trust
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The erosion of local ownership happens quietly, one closed shop at a time.
example_sentences: There has been a real erosion of trust in what we are told.
The erosion of job security accompanied the shift to short contracts.

word_family.note: the verb, used of both soil and abstract things

contexts.text: The erosion of local ownership happens quietly, one closed shop at a time.
There has been a real erosion of trust in what we are told.
The erosion of job security accompanied the shift to short contracts.

confusables.difference: Erosion says something is being worn away from outside, slowly and by pressure. Decline just says it is getting smaller or worse.
minimal_pair: The erosion of union membership followed each reform.
The decline in membership began after 1990.

entry_json.avoid: Erosion of X, never erosion in X.

entry_json.definition: given by each side to the other, on equal terms
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The two countries signed a reciprocal arrangement on healthcare for travellers.
example_sentences: It has to be reciprocal, otherwise one side just ends up doing all the giving.
Reciprocal recognition of qualifications removed a long-standing barrier for engineers.

word_family.note: to respond by doing the same thing back

contexts.text: The two countries signed a reciprocal arrangement on healthcare for travellers.
It has to be reciprocal, otherwise one side just ends up doing all the giving.
Reciprocal recognition of qualifications removed a long-standing barrier for engineers.

confusables.difference: Mutual says both sides feel or share something. Reciprocal says each side actually gives the other something in return.
minimal_pair: They share a mutual respect.
The states have a reciprocal tax treaty.

entry_json.avoid: Not used of feelings. Say mutual respect, not reciprocal respect.

entry_json.definition: a company that is owned or controlled by a larger parent company
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The profits are declared by a subsidiary registered in a country the firm barely trades in.
example_sentences: She works for a subsidiary of one of the big carmakers.
Each overseas subsidiary files its own accounts under local law.

contexts.text: The profits are declared by a subsidiary registered in a country the firm barely trades in.
She works for a subsidiary of one of the big carmakers.
Each overseas subsidiary files its own accounts under local law.

confusables.difference: A subsidiary is a separate legal company with its own accounts. A branch is just another office of the same company.
minimal_pair: The subsidiary was sold to a rival.
The branch in Leeds closed last year.

entry_json.avoid: As a noun it means the company. The adjective subsidiary meaning less important is a different word.

entry_json.definition: the ability of people to move, either from place to place or from one social level to another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap flights raised mobility for some travellers and left others exactly where they were.
example_sentences: There is much less mobility now than my parents had, in terms of what job you can end up in.
Social mobility fell in every region covered by the study.

word_family.note: to gather resources or people for action

contexts.text: Cheap flights raised mobility for some travellers and left others exactly where they were.
There is much less mobility now than my parents had, in terms of what job you can end up in.
Social mobility fell in every region covered by the study.

confusables.difference: Mobility is the capacity to move. Migration is the movement that actually happens.
minimal_pair: Labour mobility is limited by housing costs.
Migration to the capital continued all decade.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable here. Not mobilities.

entry_json.definition: interested only in your own group or country and unwilling to consider outside ideas
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A country can be well connected and still be insular in the way it thinks.
example_sentences: The town felt a bit insular to me at first, though people warmed up.
Insular hiring practices leave organisations unable to see their own blind spots.

contexts.text: A country can be well connected and still be insular in the way it thinks.
The town felt a bit insular to me at first, though people warmed up.
Insular hiring practices leave organisations unable to see their own blind spots.

confusables.difference: Insular is a choice and a criticism of an attitude. Isolated is a circumstance and carries no blame.
minimal_pair: The committee had grown insular.
The village is isolated by winter snow.

entry_json.avoid: Not about islands in modern use. Do not write insular country meaning island country.

entry_json.definition: the position of having more power or influence than anyone else in a field
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The dominance of a handful of platforms shapes what most of the world reads.
example_sentences: Their dominance in that sport went on for about fifteen years.
Market dominance allowed the firm to set terms that smaller suppliers could not refuse.

word_family.note: to have or exert that power

contexts.text: The dominance of a handful of platforms shapes what most of the world reads.
Their dominance in that sport went on for about fifteen years.
Market dominance allowed the firm to set terms that smaller suppliers could not refuse.

confusables.difference: Dominance is having most of the power. Monopoly is a technical term for having all of it, with no competitor at all.
minimal_pair: Its dominance of the market worried regulators.
The state held a monopoly on rail freight.

entry_json.avoid: Dominance of or dominance in. Not dominance on.

entry_json.definition: a situation in which everyone competes under the same rules and nobody has an unfair advantage
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Smaller producers cannot survive without a level playing field on tariffs.
example_sentences: All the unions are asking for is a level playing field when contracts go out.
Subsidies to one sector make a level playing field impossible to maintain.

chunk.shape: create X on a level playing field

contexts.text: Smaller producers cannot survive without a level playing field on tariffs.
All the unions are asking for is a level playing field when contracts go out.
Subsidies to one sector make a level playing field impossible to maintain.

confusables.difference: A level playing field is about the rules being equal before anyone starts. Fair competition describes how people behave once it has started.
minimal_pair: Tariffs destroy a level playing field.
The regulator promotes fair competition between suppliers.

entry_json.avoid: Keep the article. Not "we want level playing field".

entry_json.definition: a situation where countries or firms keep cutting standards or wages to undercut each other
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Competing purely on labour costs sets off a race to the bottom that nobody eventually wins.
example_sentences: It just becomes a race to the bottom, and the people at the end of the chain pay for it.
Environmental rules were weakened in what commentators described as a race to the bottom.
collocations: trigger a race to the bottom
a race to the bottom on wages
avoid a race to the bottom

chunk.shape: a race to the bottom on X

contexts.text: Competing purely on labour costs sets off a race to the bottom that nobody eventually wins.
It just becomes a race to the bottom, and the people at the end of the chain pay for it.
Environmental rules were weakened in what commentators described as a race to the bottom.

confusables.difference: A race to the bottom is a slide in standards over years. A price war is a short fight over price alone.
minimal_pair: Deregulation began a race to the bottom on safety.
The supermarkets started a price war before Christmas.

entry_json.avoid: Not a race to the top. The fixed phrase only runs downwards.

entry_json.definition: the loss of skilled and educated people who leave a country for better prospects abroad
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The brain drain costs the state twice, since it trains the graduates and then loses them.
example_sentences: There has been a bit of a brain drain from our region, honestly.
Nurse recruitment abroad has produced a measurable brain drain in several countries.

chunk.shape: a brain drain from X to Y

contexts.text: The brain drain costs the state twice, since it trains the graduates and then loses them.
There has been a bit of a brain drain from our region, honestly.
Nurse recruitment abroad has produced a measurable brain drain in several countries.

confusables.difference: Brain drain names the loss of skill and is always negative. Emigration is a neutral word for people leaving.
minimal_pair: The brain drain left hospitals short of specialists.
Emigration peaked in the years after the war.

entry_json.avoid: Usually with the. Not "brain drains" in the plural.

entry_json.definition: the idea that a country should produce what it can make relatively more cheaply than others
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Trade theory rests on comparative advantage rather than on being better at everything.
example_sentences: Basically each country does what it is relatively good at, which is comparative advantage.
Comparative advantage predicts specialisation but says nothing about who keeps the gains.

contexts.text: Trade theory rests on comparative advantage rather than on being better at everything.
Basically each country does what it is relatively good at, which is comparative advantage.
Comparative advantage predicts specialisation but says nothing about who keeps the gains.

confusables.difference: Comparative advantage is about what a country gives up to produce something. Competitive advantage is about what one firm does better than its rivals.
minimal_pair: The island has a comparative advantage in fishing.
The firm's competitive advantage lies in its delivery times.

entry_json.avoid: Comparative advantage in a product, not comparative advantage of.

entry_json.definition: any tax, quota or rule that makes it harder to sell goods into another country
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Removing one trade barrier often reveals three others that nobody had counted.
example_sentences: The paperwork is the real trade barrier for a business our size.
Non-tariff trade barriers now matter more than tariffs in most sectors.

contexts.text: Removing one trade barrier often reveals three others that nobody had counted.
The paperwork is the real trade barrier for a business our size.
Non-tariff trade barriers now matter more than tariffs in most sectors.

confusables.difference: A tariff is one specific kind of trade barrier, namely a tax at the border. Trade barrier is the umbrella term and includes rules and quotas.
minimal_pair: Quotas are a trade barrier that tariffs do not cover.
The tariff on steel rose to fourteen per cent.

entry_json.avoid: Countable. Say trade barriers, not trade barrier in general statements.

entry_json.definition: money put into a country by a foreign company to build or buy something lasting there
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Foreign direct investment built the plant, but the design work stayed overseas.
example_sentences: We were told foreign direct investment would bring jobs, and to be fair some came.
Foreign direct investment into the region tripled between 2004 and 2012.

contexts.text: Foreign direct investment built the plant, but the design work stayed overseas.
We were told foreign direct investment would bring jobs, and to be fair some came.
Foreign direct investment into the region tripled between 2004 and 2012.

confusables.difference: Foreign direct investment is commercial and expects a return. Aid is a transfer that does not.
minimal_pair: Foreign direct investment followed the tax reform.
Aid was suspended after the floods.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not foreign direct investments.

entry_json.definition: to allow outsiders, ideas or competition into a place or market that was previously closed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: When an economy open up to foreign competition, the adjustment falls unevenly.
example_sentences: The country really opened up to tourism about twenty years ago.
Higher education was opened up to private providers under the 2010 reforms.

contexts.text: When an economy open up to foreign competition, the adjustment falls unevenly.
The country really opened up to tourism about twenty years ago.
Higher education was opened up to private providers under the 2010 reforms.

confusables.difference: Open up to takes what is coming in and adds the sense of a barrier being lifted. Open on its own just describes the state.
minimal_pair: The market opened up to imports in 2001.
The office opens at eight.

entry_json.avoid: Keep both particles. Not "open to competition" if you mean the change.

entry_json.definition: to start making use of a supply of something valuable that is already there
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Exporters that tap into regional demand are less exposed when one market falters.
example_sentences: They managed to tap into a whole audience nobody else was talking to.
The programme tapped into skills that migrants already possessed but could not certify.

contexts.text: Exporters that tap into regional demand are less exposed when one market falters.
They managed to tap into a whole audience nobody else was talking to.
The programme tapped into skills that migrants already possessed but could not certify.

confusables.difference: Tap into is positive and means using something that was going unused. Exploit often means using it unfairly.
minimal_pair: The firm tapped into rural demand.
The firm exploited a loophole in the rules.

entry_json.avoid: Followed by a noun, never by that.

entry_json.definition: completely unable to protect yourself from the power of someone or something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Growers who sell to a single buyer are at the mercy of whatever price that buyer sets.
example_sentences: Without a contract you are basically at the mercy of whoever is scheduling the shifts.
Small importers remain at the mercy of exchange rate movements they cannot hedge against.
collocations: at the mercy of the market
leave someone at the mercy of
at the mercy of the weather

chunk.shape: X is at the mercy of Y

contexts.text: Growers who sell to a single buyer are at the mercy of whatever price that buyer sets.
Without a contract you are basically at the mercy of whoever is scheduling the shifts.
Small importers remain at the mercy of exchange rate movements they cannot hedge against.

confusables.difference: At the mercy of says you have no protection and the other side has all the power. Dependent on is neutral and simply says you need it.
minimal_pair: Farmers are at the mercy of the rains.
The village is dependent on one bus route.

entry_json.avoid: Always the mercy. Not "at mercy of".

entry_json.definition: closely together, so that one thing happens alongside the other
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rising exports and rising inequality have gone hand in hand in several economies.
example_sentences: For me the two things go hand in hand, you cannot really separate them.
Urban growth and pressure on water supply move hand in hand in the arid north.

chunk.shape: X goes hand in hand with Y

contexts.text: Rising exports and rising inequality have gone hand in hand in several economies.
For me the two things go hand in hand, you cannot really separate them.
Urban growth and pressure on water supply move hand in hand in the arid north.

confusables.difference: Hand in hand claims the two are connected. At the same time only says they overlap in time.
minimal_pair: Deregulation and risk went hand in hand.
She was studying and working at the same time.

entry_json.avoid: No articles inside the phrase. Not "hand in the hand".

entry_json.definition: to receive far more of something than can be dealt with
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Local markets are flooded with imported goods sold below the cost of making them.
example_sentences: After the piece went out we were flooded with messages for about a week.
Emergency departments are flooded with cases during each winter peak.

contexts.text: Local markets are flooded with imported goods sold below the cost of making them.
After the piece went out we were flooded with messages for about a week.
Emergency departments are flooded with cases during each winter peak.

confusables.difference: Be flooded with says the amount arrived suddenly and is too much to handle. Be full of just says there is a lot.
minimal_pair: The market was flooded with cheap steel.
The report is full of useful detail.

entry_json.avoid: Passive only in this sense. Not "imports flooded the market with".

entry_json.definition: workers who can be employed for low wages, seen as an economic resource
entry_json.own_context_sentence: An economy built on cheap labour has little reason to invest in the machines that would replace it.
example_sentences: The whole model depends on cheap labour somewhere down the line.
Access to cheap labour delayed automation in the sector by at least a decade.

contexts.text: An economy built on cheap labour has little reason to invest in the machines that would replace it.
The whole model depends on cheap labour somewhere down the line.
Access to cheap labour delayed automation in the sector by at least a decade.

confusables.difference: Cheap labour looks at workers from the employer's side as a cost. Low pay looks at the same fact from the worker's side.
minimal_pair: The region offered cheap labour.
Low pay forced many into a second job.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable and slightly cold in tone. Never "a cheap labour".

entry_json.definition: the right or ability to sell goods and services in another country
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Market access was traded away in exchange for concessions on farming.
example_sentences: Without market access there is not much point having the factory at all.
Preferential market access shaped the export mix of the smaller partners.

contexts.text: Market access was traded away in exchange for concessions on farming.
Without market access there is not much point having the factory at all.
Preferential market access shaped the export mix of the smaller partners.

confusables.difference: Market access is one country being allowed in. Free trade is the wider arrangement in which barriers come down on both sides.
minimal_pair: The deal granted market access for dairy.
Free trade between the two states began in 1993.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Say market access for a product, not to a product.

entry_json.definition: happening between two countries or involving the movement of things between them
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cross-border payments still cost more than they should in most corridors.
example_sentences: There is a lot of cross-border shopping where I grew up, because prices differ.
Cross-border enforcement remains the weak point in tackling online fraud.

contexts.text: Cross-border payments still cost more than they should in most corridors.
There is a lot of cross-border shopping where I grew up, because prices differ.
Cross-border enforcement remains the weak point in tackling online fraud.

confusables.difference: Cross-border stresses crossing a land or legal boundary between neighbours. Overseas simply means abroad, usually far away.
minimal_pair: Cross-border commuting is common here.
She spent two years working overseas.

entry_json.avoid: Attributive only. Do not write "the trade is cross-border".

entry_json.definition: across the whole world rather than in one place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A problem of this kind can only be solved on a global scale.
example_sentences: You start seeing the same brands on a global scale, which is quite strange.
Vaccine distribution was managed on a global scale for the first time.

contexts.text: A problem of this kind can only be solved on a global scale.
You start seeing the same brands on a global scale, which is quite strange.
Vaccine distribution was managed on a global scale for the first time.

confusables.difference: On a global scale is a phrase you can end a clause with, and it stresses size. Globally is a single adverb that usually sits before or after the verb.
minimal_pair: Emissions must be cut on a global scale.
The company operates globally.

entry_json.avoid: Keep the article. Not "on global scale".

entry_json.definition: a situation in which both sides must give something, not only one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Integration is a two-way street, and the receiving society has obligations of its own.
example_sentences: Respect is a two-way street, as my grandmother used to say.
Knowledge transfer proved to be a two-way street in the partnership.

contexts.text: Integration is a two-way street, and the receiving society has obligations of its own.
Respect is a two-way street, as my grandmother used to say.
Knowledge transfer proved to be a two-way street in the partnership.

confusables.difference: A two-way street is a spoken image and is used to argue that one side is doing all the work. Mutual is a plain adjective with no complaint in it.
minimal_pair: Loyalty has to be a two-way street.
They reached a mutual agreement.

entry_json.definition: the process by which separate national economies join into one larger market

entry_json.definition: a system in which staff have no fixed desk and use whichever one is free

entry_json.definition: to accept a new job, task or responsibility
