contexts.text: High turnover hides its real cost in the time experienced staff spend training replacements.
The turnover in that department is unbelievable.
Staff turnover was highest in the lowest paid grades.

confusables.difference: Turnover counts everyone who leaves, including those replaced. Attrition means the post was not filled again.
minimal_pair: Turnover was thirty per cent last year.
The team shrank through attrition.

entry_json.avoid: Turnover also means a company's total sales. Say staff turnover when the context is not obvious.

entry_json.definition: not favouring one side, so that a report treats every party equally
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A broadcaster can be impartial between parties and still be unfair to the question.
example_sentences: I want the news to be impartial, and I am not sure it ever fully is.
Coverage was assessed for whether it remained impartial across the whole campaign.

contexts.text: A broadcaster can be impartial between parties and still be unfair to the question.
I want the news to be impartial, and I am not sure it ever fully is.
Coverage was assessed for whether it remained impartial across the whole campaign.

confusables.difference: Objective is about the facts being right regardless of who is involved. Impartial is about treating the sides evenly. A report can be impartial and still get the facts wrong.
minimal_pair: The panel was impartial between the two bids.
The measurement was objective and repeatable.

entry_json.avoid: Impartial between parties, or impartial in a dispute. Not impartial to.

entry_json.definition: to report something in a way that makes it sound more shocking than it is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Outlets that sensationalise rare events leave readers badly calibrated about common ones.
example_sentences: They completely sensationalised that story, it was nothing like that.
Health scares were sensationalised in ways the underlying research did not support.

contexts.text: Outlets that sensationalise rare events leave readers badly calibrated about common ones.
They completely sensationalised that story, it was nothing like that.
Health scares were sensationalised in ways the underlying research did not support.

confusables.difference: Exaggerate is about size, saying the number was bigger. Sensationalise is about emotion, making it feel more dramatic than it was.
minimal_pair: The tabloid sensationalised the verdict.
He exaggerated how long the queue was.

entry_json.avoid: Transitive. Not "the story sensationalised".

entry_json.definition: the quality of being believed and trusted by an audience
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Credibility is lost in a single evening and rebuilt over several years.
example_sentences: Once a channel loses its credibility with me, I just stop watching.
Perceived credibility fell sharpest among readers under thirty.

contexts.text: Credibility is lost in a single evening and rebuilt over several years.
Once a channel loses its credibility with me, I just stop watching.
Perceived credibility fell sharpest among readers under thirty.

confusables.difference: Popularity is how many people choose it. Credibility is whether they believe it. A source can have one without the other.
minimal_pair: The paper kept its credibility after the correction.
The show's popularity peaked in its third season.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Credibility with an audience, not credibility to.

entry_json.definition: a system that blocks online content unless the reader has paid a subscription
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Putting careful reporting behind a paywall leaves the free tier to whoever is loudest.
example_sentences: I hit a paywall halfway through the article and gave up.
Titles that introduced a paywall reported lower traffic and higher revenue per reader.

contexts.text: Putting careful reporting behind a paywall leaves the free tier to whoever is loudest.
I hit a paywall halfway through the article and gave up.
Titles that introduced a paywall reported lower traffic and higher revenue per reader.

confusables.difference: A subscription is what the reader buys. A paywall is the barrier that makes them buy it.
minimal_pair: The report is behind a paywall.
Her subscription renews in March.

entry_json.avoid: Countable. Behind a paywall, not inside one.

entry_json.definition: the version of events that a story or a group settles on and repeats
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Once a narrative takes hold, later facts are read as confirmation of it.
example_sentences: The whole narrative around that industry has changed in five years.
Competing narratives about the cause appeared within days of the incident.

contexts.text: Once a narrative takes hold, later facts are read as confirmation of it.
The whole narrative around that industry has changed in five years.
Competing narratives about the cause appeared within days of the incident.

confusables.difference: A story is one report of what happened. A narrative is the frame that many stories are fitted into.
minimal_pair: The narrative of decline shaped every headline.
The story ran for three days.

entry_json.avoid: Countable in this sense. Not "the narrative" without saying whose.

entry_json.definition: to examine something very carefully in order to find problems in it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Claims that flatter the reader are scrutinised least.
example_sentences: Every word you put online now gets scrutinised by someone.
The methodology was scrutinised by two independent reviewers before publication.

contexts.text: Claims that flatter the reader are scrutinised least.
Every word you put online now gets scrutinised by someone.
The methodology was scrutinised by two independent reviewers before publication.

confusables.difference: Examine is neutral and can be routine. Scrutinise implies suspicion and unusual care.
minimal_pair: The accounts were scrutinised line by line.
The doctor examined her ankle.

entry_json.avoid: Transitive. Scrutinise a claim, not scrutinise over a claim.

entry_json.definition: a personal reason to want one outcome, usually financial and usually hidden
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Readers cannot weigh a claim without knowing who has a vested interest in it.
example_sentences: You have to ask who has a vested interest before you believe any of it.
Authors were required to declare any vested interest in the products tested.

contexts.text: Readers cannot weigh a claim without knowing who has a vested interest in it.
You have to ask who has a vested interest before you believe any of it.
Authors were required to declare any vested interest in the products tested.

confusables.difference: Bias is a leaning that may be unconscious. A vested interest is a concrete stake, usually money, and it is deliberate.
minimal_pair: The consultancy had a vested interest in the finding.
The sample showed a bias towards urban households.

entry_json.avoid: A vested interest in something, never a vested interest of.

entry_json.definition: a space where people hear only opinions like their own, so those opinions get louder
entry_json.own_context_sentence: An echo chamber does not persuade anyone new, it only raises the confidence of those already inside.
example_sentences: I try to follow people I disagree with so I am not stuck in an echo chamber.
Users in a strong echo chamber were less able to state the opposing case accurately.

contexts.text: An echo chamber does not persuade anyone new, it only raises the confidence of those already inside.
I try to follow people I disagree with so I am not stuck in an echo chamber.
Users in a strong echo chamber were less able to state the opposing case accurately.

confusables.difference: A filter bubble is made for you by an algorithm without your choosing. An echo chamber is one you enter by choosing your own company.
minimal_pair: The forum became an echo chamber.
The filter bubble showed her only one side of the story.

entry_json.avoid: Countable. Say in an echo chamber, not inside the echo chamber.

entry_json.definition: to force someone in power to explain and answer for what they have done
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A press that cannot hold to account the people who fund it is doing something else.
example_sentences: Somebody has to hold to account the companies dumping into that river.
Regulators were criticised for failing to hold to account firms that had breached the code.

chunk.shape: hold X to account for Y

contexts.text: A press that cannot hold to account the people who fund it is doing something else.
Somebody has to hold to account the companies dumping into that river.
Regulators were criticised for failing to hold to account firms that had breached the code.

confusables.difference: Blame assigns fault and stops there. Hold to account demands an explanation and a consequence.
minimal_pair: The committee held the board to account.
Nobody blamed the drivers.

entry_json.avoid: The object goes in the middle. Say hold ministers to account, not hold to account ministers.

entry_json.definition: to be the first to report something that was not publicly known
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The outlet that breaks a story rarely owns it by the second day.
example_sentences: A local paper actually broke a story that ended up everywhere.
Investigative teams break a story months after the first document reaches them.
collocations: be the first to break it

contexts.text: The outlet that breaks a story rarely owns it by the second day.
A local paper actually broke a story that ended up everywhere.
Investigative teams break a story months after the first document reaches them.

confusables.difference: Report is what everyone does once the story is out. Break a story means being first, before anyone else has it.
minimal_pair: The magazine broke the story in April.
Every channel reported it by the evening.

entry_json.avoid: Break in this sense is only about being first. Not the same as breaking news, which is any urgent item.

vocab_new.lemma: take with a pinch of salt

entry_json.headword: take with a pinch of salt
entry_json.ipa: teɪk wɪð ə pɪntʃ əv sɔːlt
entry_json.definition: to treat a claim as probably exaggerated and not to believe all of it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Survey figures repeated without a method should be take with a pinch of salt.
example_sentences: I take with a pinch of salt anything that gets shared that fast.
Self-reported hours must be take with a pinch of salt in any workload study.
collocations: take it with a pinch of salt
taken with a pinch of salt
treat with a pinch of salt

chunk.shape: take X with a pinch of salt

contexts.text: Survey figures repeated without a method should be take with a pinch of salt.
contexts.gap_span: take with a pinch of salt

contexts.text: I take with a pinch of salt anything that gets shared that fast.
contexts.gap_span: take with a pinch of salt

contexts.text: Self-reported hours must be take with a pinch of salt in any workload study.
contexts.gap_span: take with a pinch of salt

confusables.difference: Doubt is a plain statement that you are unsure. Take with a pinch of salt is spoken, milder and slightly humorous.
minimal_pair: Take the ratings with a pinch of salt.
I doubt the figures are accurate.

entry_json.avoid: British form is pinch. American English says grain.

entry_json.definition: to decide what happened before you have enough evidence
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Early coverage of an incident invites readers to jump to conclusions that later reporting must undo.
example_sentences: I do not want to jump to conclusions before we hear from her.
Reviewers are trained not to jump to conclusions from a single trial.

contexts.text: Early coverage of an incident invites readers to jump to conclusions that later reporting must undo.
I do not want to jump to conclusions before we hear from her.
Reviewers are trained not to jump to conclusions from a single trial.

confusables.difference: Assume can be reasonable and even necessary. Jump to conclusions says you moved too fast on too little.
minimal_pair: The report jumped to conclusions about the cause.
The model assumes constant demand.

entry_json.avoid: Plural conclusions. Not "jump to a conclusion" in the fixed phrase.

entry_json.definition: reporting that takes months of digging to uncover something powerful people wanted hidden
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Investigative journalism costs more per story than any other kind and sells fewer copies.
example_sentences: Proper investigative journalism is what I would actually pay for.
Funding for investigative journalism shifted from newspapers to charitable foundations.

contexts.text: Investigative journalism costs more per story than any other kind and sells fewer copies.
Proper investigative journalism is what I would actually pay for.
Funding for investigative journalism shifted from newspapers to charitable foundations.

confusables.difference: Reporting covers what has already happened and is publicly available. Investigative journalism uncovers what was concealed.
minimal_pair: Investigative journalism exposed the contracts.
Reporting on the match filled two pages.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. A piece of investigative journalism when you mean one story.

entry_json.definition: the consistent position an outlet takes on issues, decided by its editors
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Every outlet has an editorial line, and the honest ones say what theirs is.
example_sentences: You can guess their editorial line from the headline alone.
The editorial line on planning reform remained unchanged across three editors.

contexts.text: Every outlet has an editorial line, and the honest ones say what theirs is.
You can guess their editorial line from the headline alone.
The editorial line on planning reform remained unchanged across three editors.

confusables.difference: Editorial independence is freedom from the owner or the state. An editorial line is the view the editors themselves choose. A paper can have both.
minimal_pair: Its editorial line favours deregulation.
Editorial independence was written into the trust deed.

entry_json.avoid: Countable. Not editorial lines for one outlet.

entry_json.definition: the large established news organisations, as opposed to independent or online ones
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Attacks on the mainstream media often come from outlets that are themselves very large.
example_sentences: I get most of my news outside the mainstream media now.
Trust in mainstream media declined more slowly than trust in social platforms.

contexts.text: Attacks on the mainstream media often come from outlets that are themselves very large.
I get most of my news outside the mainstream media now.
Trust in mainstream media declined more slowly than trust in social platforms.

confusables.difference: Social media is the platform where anyone can publish. Mainstream media is the set of established organisations with editors.
minimal_pair: The mainstream media ignored the protest for a week.
Social media carried it within hours.

entry_json.avoid: Media takes a singular verb in modern British usage. Say the media is, not the media are.

entry_json.definition: a title written to make people click rather than to describe the article
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A clickbait headline wins the click and loses the reader on the second paragraph.
example_sentences: I fall for a clickbait headline about once a week.
Articles with a clickbait headline showed higher entry and far lower completion.

contexts.text: A clickbait headline wins the click and loses the reader on the second paragraph.
I fall for a clickbait headline about once a week.
Articles with a clickbait headline showed higher entry and far lower completion.

confusables.difference: A misleading headline says something untrue. A clickbait headline may be technically true and simply withholds the point to make you click.
minimal_pair: The clickbait headline hid the answer until the last line.
The misleading headline stated a figure the article contradicted.

entry_json.avoid: Countable. Clickbait alone is uncountable.

entry_json.definition: to check whether the claims in a statement or article are actually true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Claims are fact-checked most thoroughly when they are least likely to be believed anyway.
example_sentences: I always fact-check anything before I share it now.
Statements were fact-checked against the original transcripts.

contexts.text: Claims are fact-checked most thoroughly when they are least likely to be believed anyway.
I always fact-check anything before I share it now.
Statements were fact-checked against the original transcripts.

confusables.difference: Verify means confirming something is true and stops there. Fact-check means testing a specific published claim, which may end in a correction.
minimal_pair: The team fact-checked every figure in the speech.
The bank verified her identity.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenated as a verb. The noun is fact-checking.

entry_json.definition: to spread extremely quickly online as people share it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Content that goes viral is optimised for sharing rather than for being right.
example_sentences: A video of the fox in our garden went viral, which was surreal.
Posts that went viral were shorter and more emotional than the average in the sample.

contexts.text: Content that goes viral is optimised for sharing rather than for being right.
A video of the fox in our garden went viral, which was surreal.
Posts that went viral were shorter and more emotional than the average in the sample.

confusables.difference: Become popular is slow and can last. Go viral is sudden, driven by sharing, and usually short-lived.
minimal_pair: The clip went viral in two days.
The band became popular over several years.

entry_json.avoid: Go, not become, in this fixed phrase. Not "went virally".

entry_json.definition: the amount of space a story is given in print, used as a measure of attention
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The two events received column inches in inverse proportion to the number of people affected.
example_sentences: That story got more column inches than anything else that month.
Column inches devoted to each policy area were counted across six titles.

contexts.text: The two events received column inches in inverse proportion to the number of people affected.
That story got more column inches than anything else that month.
Column inches devoted to each policy area were counted across six titles.

confusables.difference: Coverage is the general word for how much attention a story gets in any medium. Column inches is specifically print and is a countable measure.
minimal_pair: The trial filled column inches for a fortnight.
Coverage of the strike was heavy on radio.

entry_json.avoid: Plural only. Not a column inch except in technical printing use.

entry_json.definition: to decide which issues everyone else ends up discussing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Outlets do not tell readers what to think so much as set the agenda about what to think about.
example_sentences: Whoever gets there first tends to set the agenda for the whole week.
Editors set the agenda through selection rather than through commentary.

contexts.text: Outlets do not tell readers what to think so much as set the agenda about what to think about.
Whoever gets there first tends to set the agenda for the whole week.
Editors set the agenda through selection rather than through commentary.

confusables.difference: Influence is any effect on what people think. Setting the agenda is narrower and stronger, choosing which topics get discussed at all.
minimal_pair: The paper set the agenda for the debate.
The advertisement influenced her choice.

entry_json.avoid: Always the agenda. Not "set an agenda" when you mean public debate.

entry_json.definition: without being noticed by the people who might have objected
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Two large mergers went through under the radar while attention was elsewhere.
example_sentences: That band stayed under the radar for years before anyone noticed.
The rule change passed under the radar during a heavy news week.

contexts.text: Two large mergers went through under the radar while attention was elsewhere.
That band stayed under the radar for years before anyone noticed.
The rule change passed under the radar during a heavy news week.

confusables.difference: In secret means somebody deliberately hid it. Under the radar can mean it was simply not noticed, with nobody hiding anything.
minimal_pair: The change passed under the radar.
The meeting was held in secret.

entry_json.avoid: Informal. Keep the radar, never a radar.

entry_json.definition: to treat something small as if it were far more serious than it is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rare incidents are routinely blown out of proportion because they make better copy.
example_sentences: The whole thing got blown out of proportion and it was really nothing.
Risks with low absolute frequency were blown out of proportion in the coverage sampled.

contexts.text: Rare incidents are routinely blown out of proportion because they make better copy.
The whole thing got blown out of proportion and it was really nothing.
Risks with low absolute frequency were blown out of proportion in the coverage sampled.

confusables.difference: Exaggerate is about a single claim being overstated. Blow out of proportion is about the whole reaction being too big for the event.
minimal_pair: The story was blown out of proportion.
He exaggerated the cost by a hundred pounds.

entry_json.avoid: Usually passive. Add all for emphasis, as in out of all proportion.

entry_json.definition: reporting that continues without a break, day and night
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Round-the-clock coverage fills the hours between developments with speculation.
example_sentences: There was round-the-clock coverage for about four days and then nothing.
Round-the-clock coverage of the emergency began within an hour of the first alert.

contexts.text: Round-the-clock coverage fills the hours between developments with speculation.
There was round-the-clock coverage for about four days and then nothing.
Round-the-clock coverage of the emergency began within an hour of the first alert.

confusables.difference: Live coverage is happening now and may last an hour. Round-the-clock coverage continues for days without stopping.
minimal_pair: Round-the-clock coverage ran for a week.
Live coverage begins at eight.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Hyphenate round-the-clock before the noun.

entry_json.definition: someone or something that almost everyone in a country has heard of
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Two decades of advertising turned a regional brand into a household name.
example_sentences: She was a household name when I was growing up.
The programme made a household name of a researcher who had published for years unnoticed.

contexts.text: Two decades of advertising turned a regional brand into a household name.
She was a household name when I was growing up.
The programme made a household name of a researcher who had published for years unnoticed.

confusables.difference: Famous is a general adjective and can describe any level of fame. A household name specifically means ordinary people in ordinary homes know it.
minimal_pair: The company became a household name.
The chef is famous among other chefs.

entry_json.avoid: Keep the article and the singular. Not "household names" of one person.

entry_json.definition: to influence what most people in a society come to believe about an issue
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Repetition shape public opinion more reliably than argument does.
example_sentences: Adverts definitely shape public opinion, even when you think they do not.
Coverage shape public opinion on the policy well before any vote took place.

contexts.text: Repetition shape public opinion more reliably than argument does.
Adverts definitely shape public opinion, even when you think they do not.
Coverage shape public opinion on the policy well before any vote took place.

confusables.difference: Shaping public opinion is changing what people think. Reporting it is describing what they already thought. Confusing the two is the core criticism of polling coverage.
minimal_pair: The campaign shaped public opinion on rents.
The survey reported public opinion on rents.

entry_json.avoid: Public opinion is uncountable and singular. Not public opinions.

entry_json.definition: a day when little of importance happens, so minor stories get unusual attention
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Stories that would vanish in a busy week survive on a slow news day.
example_sentences: It must have been a slow news day for that to be the front page.
Minor items received disproportionate space on what the editors called a slow news day.
collocations: it was a slow news day

contexts.text: Stories that would vanish in a busy week survive on a slow news day.
It must have been a slow news day for that to be the front page.
Minor items received disproportionate space on what the editors called a slow news day.

confusables.difference: A quiet period is neutral and can describe any activity. A slow news day is specifically about the newsroom and is faintly mocking.
minimal_pair: It ran only because it was a slow news day.
Sales enter a quiet period after Christmas.

entry_json.avoid: News is uncountable. Not "slow news days" when describing one occasion.

entry_json.definition: the state of having so much information available that none of it can be processed properly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Information overload does not make people better informed, it makes them tired.
example_sentences: I get information overload just from my phone in the morning.
Information overload was associated with lower recall of any individual item.

contexts.text: Information overload does not make people better informed, it makes them tired.
I get information overload just from my phone in the morning.
Information overload was associated with lower recall of any individual item.

confusables.difference: Misinformation is false content. Information overload is too much content, true or false. The remedies are completely different.
minimal_pair: Information overload left readers unable to prioritise.
Misinformation about the vaccine spread through group chats.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not information overloads.

entry_json.definition: a very short extract from a speech, chosen because it is quotable rather than complete
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Complex policy survives badly once it has been reduced to a soundbite.
example_sentences: All you ever hear is the soundbite, never the full answer.
Broadcast soundbite length fell steadily across the four decades studied.

contexts.text: Complex policy survives badly once it has been reduced to a soundbite.
All you ever hear is the soundbite, never the full answer.
Broadcast soundbite length fell steadily across the four decades studied.

confusables.difference: A quotation is any passage repeated word for word, of any length. A soundbite is short by design and chosen for how it sounds.
minimal_pair: The soundbite lasted nine seconds.
The quotation ran to a full paragraph.

entry_json.avoid: Countable. One word in British usage.

entry_json.definition: the right of journalists to report without control or punishment by the state
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Press freedom is tested by what may be published about the powerful, not about the weak.
example_sentences: Press freedom is something you only notice when it goes.
Press freedom indicators declined in a third of the countries surveyed.

contexts.text: Press freedom is tested by what may be published about the powerful, not about the weak.
Press freedom is something you only notice when it goes.
Press freedom indicators declined in a third of the countries surveyed.

confusables.difference: Freedom of speech belongs to everyone as individuals. Press freedom is the specific protection of publishing and journalism.
minimal_pair: Press freedom protects the newsroom.
Freedom of speech protects the person on the street.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not press freedoms.

entry_json.definition: journalism that simply reworks press releases instead of doing original reporting
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Newsroom cuts produce churnalism rather than silence, which is harder to notice.
example_sentences: A lot of what I read now is just churnalism, honestly.
Churnalism was measured by comparing published copy against the originating releases.

contexts.text: Newsroom cuts produce churnalism rather than silence, which is harder to notice.
A lot of what I read now is just churnalism, honestly.
Churnalism was measured by comparing published copy against the originating releases.

confusables.difference: Churnalism reproduces what somebody else wanted published. Investigative journalism uncovers what somebody wanted hidden. They are opposite ends of the same trade.
minimal_pair: The section was pure churnalism.
Investigative journalism took eight months to produce one piece.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable and informal. Explain the term the first time you use it.

entry_json.definition: the amount of broadcast time given to a person, party or subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Equal air time between two sides can misrepresent a question where the evidence is one-sided.
example_sentences: The smaller parties get hardly any air time.
Air time allocated to each candidate was logged minute by minute.

contexts.text: Equal air time between two sides can misrepresent a question where the evidence is one-sided.
The smaller parties get hardly any air time.
Air time allocated to each candidate was logged minute by minute.

confusables.difference: Air time is broadcast minutes on radio or television. Column inches is space in print. Use the one that matches the medium.
minimal_pair: The debate received four hours of air time.
The story filled column inches for a week.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Two words in British usage, one word in some American style guides.

entry_json.definition: to be strongly criticised in public
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The regulator come under fire for approving a merger it had previously opposed.
example_sentences: The council came under fire over the parking changes.
The methodology come under fire from statisticians within a week of publication.

chunk.shape: X comes under fire for Y

contexts.text: The regulator come under fire for approving a merger it had previously opposed.
The council came under fire over the parking changes.
The methodology come under fire from statisticians within a week of publication.

confusables.difference: Be criticised is neutral and works in any register. Come under fire is stronger, more public and slightly journalistic.
minimal_pair: The board came under fire for the bonus.
The plan was criticised in the report.

entry_json.avoid: Under fire for a thing, from a person. Do not mix the two prepositions.

entry_json.definition: a public argument in which two sides attack each other in statements
entry_json.own_context_sentence: What began as a technical disagreement became a war of words conducted through press releases.
example_sentences: There has been a war of words between the two clubs all season.
A war of words between the ministries delayed the decision by three months.
collocations: escalate into a war of words

chunk.shape: a war of words between X and Y

contexts.text: What began as a technical disagreement became a war of words conducted through press releases.
There has been a war of words between the two clubs all season.
A war of words between the ministries delayed the decision by three months.

confusables.difference: A debate is structured and aims at a conclusion. A war of words is hostile and aims at winning.
minimal_pair: The exchange turned into a war of words.
The debate covered three amendments.

entry_json.avoid: Words is always plural here. Not "a war of word".

entry_json.definition: the process by which a minority group takes on the culture of the majority and loses its own
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Assimilation is often measured by language and rarely by what people lose in acquiring it.
example_sentences: My grandparents went through complete assimilation, and we lost the language in one generation.
Assimilation and integration produced different outcomes in the communities compared.

word_family.note: to absorb or be absorbed into a culture
having taken on the majority culture

contexts.text: Assimilation is often measured by language and rarely by what people lose in acquiring it.
My grandparents went through complete assimilation, and we lost the language in one generation.
Assimilation and integration produced different outcomes in the communities compared.

confusables.difference: Integration means joining the wider society while keeping your own culture. Assimilation means giving that culture up. The distinction is the whole argument.
minimal_pair: Assimilation policies banned the local language in schools.
Integration policies funded classes in both languages.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not assimilations.

entry_json.definition: real but impossible to touch or measure directly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The intangible value of a language is the reason its loss cannot be costed.
example_sentences: There is something intangible about that place that I cannot describe.
Intangible cultural heritage includes crafts, music and the knowledge behind them.

word_family.note: able to be touched or clearly measured

contexts.text: The intangible value of a language is the reason its loss cannot be costed.
There is something intangible about that place that I cannot describe.
Intangible cultural heritage includes crafts, music and the knowledge behind them.

confusables.difference: Invisible means you cannot see it but it may be physical. Intangible means it has no physical form at all.
minimal_pair: The intangible benefits included trust and reputation.
The damage was invisible from the road.

entry_json.avoid: Of qualities and value, not of objects that are simply hidden.

entry_json.definition: to bring something back into use or life after it had almost disappeared
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Languages can be revived, but only where children have a reason to use them daily.

entry_json.definition: to feel pleased and satisfied about something you or your group have done

entry_json.avoid: Countable and informal. It is a judgement, so signal that it is your opinion.

entry_json.definition: a holiday sold as one price covering travel, accommodation and often meals
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The package holiday made foreign travel affordable and made whole coastlines look the same.

entry_json.definition: a holiday of only a few days, usually to a city
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The short break replaced the fortnight and made air travel far more frequent per traveller.

We do a short break two or three times a year instead of one long holiday.
Short break bookings grew as flight prices fell and annual leave stayed flat.

The day trip left at seven and returned at nine.

entry_json.avoid: Countable. British English. Americans say a getaway.

entry_json.definition: to spend time somewhere enjoying the feeling of the place rather than doing anything
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Visitors who stop to soak up the atmosphere spend more locally than those who tick off sites.

entry_json.definition: the time of year when few visitors come and prices are lowest
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Businesses survive the low season on what they earn in eight weeks of the high one.

entry_json.definition: travelling cheaply and independently over a long period, carrying your own luggage

I went backpacking for six months after university.
Backpacking routes concentrated visitors into a narrow corridor of towns.

entry_json.definition: a move to a different place, wanted because the current one has become stale
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Sometimes what people call burnout is answered by a change of scene rather than by treatment.

contexts.text: Sometimes what people call burnout is answered by a change of scene rather than by treatment.
I just needed a change of scene for a few days.
Participants who reported wanting a change of scene scored higher on the fatigue measure.

She booked a holiday for August.

entry_json.avoid: British says scene, American often says scenery. Keep scene here.

entry_json.definition: the friendly welcome given to visitors, and the industry built on providing it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Hospitality employs more people per pound of turnover than almost any other sector.
example_sentences: The hospitality we got in that village was genuinely humbling.

contexts.text: Hospitality employs more people per pound of turnover than almost any other sector.
The hospitality we got in that village was genuinely humbling.
Employment in hospitality fell fastest and recovered slowest across the period.

confusables.difference: Service is what a business provides in exchange for payment. Hospitality is the warmth of the welcome, and it can be entirely unpaid.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Work in hospitality, not in the hospitality.

entry_json.definition: to visit or complete something quickly just so it can be counted as done

We just ticked off the main things and did not really see anything.
Visitors who tick off attractions rapidly reported lower recall a month later.

entry_json.definition: good enough to justify making the journey to see it

The market on a Saturday is well worth a visit.
The restored mill was judged well worth a visit by nine in ten respondents.

minimal_pair: The chapel is well worth a visit.
The chapel is interesting for its carvings.

entry_json.avoid: Worth takes a noun or -ing, never an infinitive. Not "worth to visit".

entry_json.definition: happening between or affecting people of different generations
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Intergenerational transfers of wealth now shape who owns a home more than earnings do.
example_sentences: There is a lot of intergenerational support in our family, it goes both ways.
Intergenerational contact was found to reduce reported loneliness in both age groups.

contexts.text: Intergenerational transfers of wealth now shape who owns a home more than earnings do.
There is a lot of intergenerational support in our family, it goes both ways.
Intergenerational contact was found to reduce reported loneliness in both age groups.

confusables.difference: Generational describes one generation and what it is like. Intergenerational describes what passes between two of them.
minimal_pair: Intergenerational lending funds most first purchases.
The generational shift in attitudes was gradual.

entry_json.avoid: Attributive. One word, no hyphen in modern British usage.

entry_json.definition: no longer in contact with a family member after a serious falling out
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Support services rarely reach the estranged, because the family is assumed to be the safety net.

contexts.text: Support services rarely reach the estranged, because the family is assumed to be the safety net.
They have been estranged for about ten years now.
Respondents estranged from a parent reported different outcomes from those simply living apart.

confusables.difference: Distant describes a relationship that is cool but continuing. Estranged means contact has stopped altogether, usually after a rupture.
minimal_pair: She has been estranged from her brother since the sale.
They have a distant but polite relationship.

entry_json.avoid: Estranged from a person. Not estranged with.

entry_json.definition: a person, usually a child or older relative, who relies on someone else financially
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Households with a dependant at each end of the age range are squeezed from both directions.

contexts.text: Households with a dependant at each end of the age range are squeezed from both directions.
I have two dependants, so I cannot just take a pay cut.
Households with at least one dependant were analysed separately in the income study.

confusables.difference: In British spelling the noun is dependant with an a, and the adjective is dependent with an e. The distinction matters in writing.
minimal_pair: She has three dependants.
She is financially dependent on her sister.

entry_json.avoid: Noun with an a in British English. American English uses dependent for both.

entry_json.definition: the network of relationships created by blood and marriage
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Kinship obligations organise care in societies where the state provides none.
example_sentences: There is a strong sense of kinship in our extended family.
Kinship structures shaped land inheritance across the three villages studied.

word_family.note: your relatives, chiefly in fixed phrases

contexts.text: Kinship obligations organise care in societies where the state provides none.
There is a strong sense of kinship in our extended family.
Kinship structures shaped land inheritance across the three villages studied.

confusables.difference: Family usually means the people you live with or are close to. Kinship is the wider structure of relatedness and includes people you have never met.
minimal_pair: Kinship links four villages through marriage.
The family gathered for the funeral.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Slightly academic in tone.

entry_json.definition: competition and jealousy between brothers and sisters
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Sibling rivalry is usually about the parents' attention rather than about the thing being fought over.
example_sentences: There was a bit of sibling rivalry between us growing up.
Sibling rivalry was reported most often in families with children close in age.

contexts.text: Sibling rivalry is usually about the parents' attention rather than about the thing being fought over.
There was a bit of sibling rivalry between us growing up.
Sibling rivalry was reported most often in families with children close in age.

confusables.difference: Conflict is the general word for a clash of any kind. Sibling rivalry is specifically competitive, between brothers and sisters, and often about attention.
minimal_pair: Sibling rivalry faded once they left home.
The conflict between the two departments lasted years.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not sibling rivalries.

entry_json.definition: the situation of parents whose children have all left home
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The empty nest arrives later in every generation as housing costs delay departure.
example_sentences: We are dealing with the empty nest at the moment and it is odd.

contexts.text: The empty nest arrives later in every generation as housing costs delay departure.
We are dealing with the empty nest at the moment and it is odd.
Parents in the empty nest stage reported an initial fall and then a rise in wellbeing.

confusables.difference: Living alone is simply a household of one. The empty nest specifically means the children have gone and the parents remain together.
minimal_pair: The empty nest changed how they used the house.
She has been living alone since the divorce.

entry_json.avoid: Usually with the. Empty nest syndrome names the difficulty of adjusting.

entry_json.definition: a family formed when two adults with children from earlier relationships live together
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A blended family negotiates rules that most households simply inherit.
example_sentences: We are a blended family, so Christmas takes some organising.
Children in a blended family showed outcomes comparable with other household types once income was controlled for.
collocations: grow up in a blended family

contexts.text: A blended family negotiates rules that most households simply inherit.
We are a blended family, so Christmas takes some organising.
Children in a blended family showed outcomes comparable with other household types once income was controlled for.

confusables.difference: An extended family is grandparents, aunts and cousins as well as parents and children. A blended family is about step-relationships formed by a new partnership.
minimal_pair: The blended family includes two stepchildren.
The extended family fills three tables at a wedding.

entry_json.avoid: Countable. Preferred to the older and colder term reconstituted family.

entry_json.definition: to raise a child and teach them how to behave
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children brought up in two languages keep both only where both are used at home.
example_sentences: I was brought up by my grandmother, mostly.
Children brought up in the same household diverged sharply once they left it.

contexts.text: Children brought up in two languages keep both only where both are used at home.
I was brought up by my grandmother, mostly.
Children brought up in the same household diverged sharply once they left it.

confusables.difference: Raise is the American preference and is now common everywhere. Bring up is the traditional British verb and is slightly more about manners and values.

She raised three children on her own.

entry_json.avoid: Separable. Bring up also means to mention a topic, which is a different sense.

entry_json.definition: to resemble an older relative in appearance or character
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children who take after a parent in temperament are often treated as though they chose it.
example_sentences: She really take after her father in that respect.
Participants who take after a parent in build were compared on activity levels.

contexts.text: Children who take after a parent in temperament are often treated as though they chose it.
She really take after her father in that respect.
Participants who take after a parent in build were compared on activity levels.

minimal_pair: He takes after his mother.
The new hall resembles the old one.

entry_json.avoid: No continuous form. Not "he is taking after his father".

entry_json.definition: to have an argument that damages a relationship

contexts.text: Families that fall out with each other over inheritance rarely recover the relationship afterwards.
I fell out with my brother about ten years ago and we barely speak.
Respondents who had fallen out with a sibling reported reduced contact with the wider family too.

confusables.difference: Argue describes one occasion and may change nothing. Fall out with means the relationship itself was damaged and contact reduced.
minimal_pair: They fell out with their cousins years ago.
They argued about the bill and then paid it.

entry_json.avoid: With a person, over a subject. Do not swap the prepositions.

entry_json.definition: to admire and respect someone, usually someone older
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children look up to whoever is nearest and consistent, not whoever is most impressive.

I always look up to my aunt, she was the one who encouraged me.
Young people who look up to an adult outside the family showed better attendance.

entry_json.definition: to speak angrily to someone because they have done something wrong

Staff who told off pupils publicly saw no improvement in later behaviour.

entry_json.definition: a duty that two or more people carry together rather than one carrying it alone

entry_json.definition: a home where one adult raises the children without a partner living there

Income after housing costs was lowest in the single-parent household group.

entry_json.definition: the bonds of duty and affection that connect members of a family

contexts.text: Family ties decide who moves for work and who stays, more reliably than salary does.
Family ties are the reason I have never moved away.
Strong family ties were associated with lower geographical mobility across the sample.

entry_json.definition: to reach the age at which a person is legally an adult

contexts.text: Young people come of age into a housing market their parents entered on very different terms.
When she came of age she moved out almost immediately.
Those who came of age during the downturn earned less for a decade afterwards.

entry_json.definition: to accept that something is your duty or your fault

contexts.text: Adults who take responsibility for an ageing parent often reduce their own hours to do it.
You have to take responsibility for your own decisions at some point.
Carers who take responsibility for a relative reported lower pension contributions over time.

confusables.difference: Be responsible for is a state and may be assigned to you. Take responsibility for is an action and means you accepted it.

She is responsible for the whole department.

entry_json.avoid: For, always. Not "take responsibility of".

entry_json.definition: the whole set of methods and reasoning behind a piece of research
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A conclusion is only as trustworthy as the methodology that produced it.

contexts.text: A conclusion is only as trustworthy as the methodology that produced it.
The methodology section is the bit I always skip and probably should not.
The methodology was published in advance so that the analysis could not be changed later.

The method used was a postal questionnaire.

entry_json.definition: the relationship where one thing actually produces another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Establishing causation requires ruling out the explanations that a correlation leaves open.

Everyone jumps from a pattern to causation far too quickly.
Causation could not be established from observational data alone.

Evidence on the long-term effect remained inconclusive across four reviews.

entry_json.definition: checked before publication by other researchers working in the same field
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Peer-reviewed does not mean correct, it means two or three specialists found no obvious fault.

Only peer-reviewed sources were included in the systematic review.

entry_json.definition: evidence that comes from observation or experiment rather than from reasoning alone

Empirical evidence on the intervention was drawn from six countries.

entry_json.definition: the range within which the true value probably lies, given the way a study was done
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A difference smaller than the margin of error is not a finding, however much it is quoted.

Results were reported with a margin of error of three percentage points.

entry_json.definition: the group in a study that does not receive the treatment, used for comparison

contexts.text: Without a control group there is nothing to compare the improvement against.
Half of them were the control group and got the standard treatment.
The control group was matched on age and background before the trial began.

entry_json.definition: to show that an explanation cannot be correct and remove it from consideration
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Good design rules out the alternative explanations before the result is announced.
example_sentences: They have ruled out an infection, so it must be something else.

contexts.text: Good design rules out the alternative explanations before the result is announced.
